extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of science, and scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating arguments and inferences based on induction and analogy, including when and how empirical or causative laws may be extended in time and place and how analogical arguments should be weighed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate ultimate and derivative laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between ultimate laws of causation and derivative uniformities (uniformities of co-existence and sequence that flow from them).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivative uniformities are 'inferior' to the ultimate laws from which they are derived: they are narrower in extent and lower in degree of certainty. Example: the general law that a cause produces an effect is more secure than a derived empirical conjunction of two effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess dependence on collocations of primeval causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a given uniformity depends on the same collocation of primeval causes; if collocations vary, derivative uniformities may fail even when ultimate laws remain true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the collocation of causes changes, 'a totally different set of derivative uniformities may, and generally will, be the result.' Example: day and night are successive effects of a common cause (earth's rotation + sun); if different collocations obtain (e.g., on sun's surface), the derivative uniformity need not hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider susceptibility to counteracting causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether additional or supervening causes might wholly or partially counteract the combined causes that produce a derivative uniformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivative laws (especially those depending on combinations of causes) are liable to frustration from several possible counteracting causes; each counteracting cause reduces the reliability of the derivative uniformity even when the underlying ultimate laws remain true.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit temporal extension of empirical/derivative laws to adjacent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend empirical or derivative (non-causative) laws cautiously into the future — trust principally adjacent cases in time; confidence weakens with temporal distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: from five thousand years' observation we can be practically certain the sun will rise tomorrow, but projecting the same law twenty thousand years ahead is much weaker because rare combinations or slow-acting causes may accumulate. The further into the future, the weaker the induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit spatial extension to regions under same causal influence
rubrics_metrics.description: When extending an empirical law to new places, require that the new cases be 'within the influence of the same individual agents' (same causal collocations or common origin).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If effects 'can be traced with any probability to an identical (and not merely a similar) origin,' we may extend the empirical law over the observed bounds, subject to possible counteracting causes. Knowing the causes allows larger spatial extension (e.g., predicting rotation for a newly found planet within the solar system).

rubrics_metrics.name: When causes are known, judge probability by known durability and chance of destruction
rubrics_metrics.description: If the actual causes of a uniformity are known, evaluate future occurrence by assessing the probabilities that those causes will persist and not be counteracted or destroyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: knowing the sun gives light and the earth rotates lets us judge the chance the sun will rise tomorrow by the probability that these causes will be destroyed or counteracted — which, given long past persistence, is negligible for adjacent times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy requires resemblance not known to be immaterial
rubrics_metrics.description: An analogical argument is only relevant when the properties shared by A and B are not known to be unconnected with the attribute m we infer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the common properties are already shown to be immaterial to m (by elimination or law), the analogy is 'put out of court.' Analogy assumes m depends on some property of A that is uncertain; B sharing some of those properties gives some probability that B has m.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength of analogy proportional to ascertained resemblance vs difference and ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: Weigh analogical inferences by the extent of confirmed resemblance compared to ascertained differences and the volume of unknown properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If B agrees with A in many known properties and differs little, the probability that B has A's derivative property m increases (example: 'nine out of ten' known properties yields a rough 9:1 expectation). But many unknowns limit confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for dissimilarities as counter-probabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat every proved dissimilarity between cases as furnishing a counter-probability against the analogical conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On average, differences in ultimate properties imply differences in derivative properties; known differences may balance or outweigh known resemblances (example: lunar differences that argue against the moon being inhabited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve conflicting analogies by weighing analogies to positive vs negative cases
rubrics_metrics.description: When a new case resembles some cases where m exists but also resembles cases where m does not, weigh the conflicting analogies to decide net probability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: amber resembling both vegetable and mineral products; a painting resembling works of two different masters. Consider whether any property is a conclusive mark established by induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analogy primarily as a guide for further investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat analogical reasoning as provisional and most valuable for suggesting experiments or observations that can produce more rigorous induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minor analogical suspicions are 'guide-posts' suggesting experiments (experimenta crucis) rather than substitutes for full induction. Hypotheses that explain facts and predict new ones are useful even if not yet confirmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not substitute belief or instinct for evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Belief in a principle (e.g., universality of causation) is not evidence; one must appeal to faculties that take cognizance of fact (sense, consciousness) rather than mere instinctive belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The universality of causation is an assumption underlying inductive methods; its acceptance on psychological grounds (everyone believes it) is not a substitute for evidence that keeps belief 'conformable to fact.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize inductive methods presuppose the law of causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods like Agreement and Difference presuppose that every event must have some cause; this assumption is built into their logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., the Method of Agreement assumes that negating every other antecedent leaves the true cause; the Method of Difference assumes that removing A while keeping other circumstances the same shows A is the cause. These rely on the universality of causation and so should be scrutinized rather than taken for granted.
